Chapter 2: Building Trust and Communication from the Ground Up
You know, every team starts out as just a bunch of individuals—each person carrying their own hopes, worries, and a unique way of looking at things. In those early days, everyone’s a little cautious, right? People are testing the waters, figuring out what’s safe to share and what’s better kept inside.
It’s in those moments that tiny misunderstandings start to pop up. Maybe someone misreads a message, or a suggestion gets ignored, or a joke just doesn’t land. It’s easy to shrug these off and say, “Ah, that’s just part of getting used to each other.” But honestly, these are the first hints of how trust and communication are going to grow—or not.
Let me tell you about an esports team I heard about. They brought in a new player halfway through the season. This guy was talented, but he kept pretty quiet, not wanting to rock the boat. He saw the team making the same mistake over and over in practice, but he stayed silent, worried about stepping on anyone’s toes.
They kept losing in the same frustrating way. Finally, after one especially tough loss, he decided to speak up. And to his surprise, the team actually listened. They were grateful for his perspective, and that moment changed everything—not just their strategy, but the way they listened to one another.
Most teams think trust and communication will just happen over time. But the truth is, they need to be built on purpose. It’s not enough to simply have ways to talk—you’ve got to make sure everyone feels safe using them. That means creating a space where people feel comfortable asking questions, giving feedback with kindness, and treating mistakes as chances to learn instead of reasons to feel embarrassed.
There was another team where the leader, frustrated by repeated slip-ups, started calling out teammates in front of everyone. The idea was to get people to improve, but the effect? The opposite. Folks got defensive. Conversations turned stiff and guarded. Performance dropped.
But things started to shift when the leader took time to sit down with each person, apologize, and ask for honest input. They began to hold regular check-ins—not just about game plans, but about how everyone was actually feeling. Little by little, trust came back, and people started to open up again.
It’s so easy to overlook the power of small gestures—a nod of encouragement, a quick message after a hard game, or just being willing to listen without judgment. Over time, these moments add up. They become the bedrock that lets a team handle all the ups and downs of competition.
Here’s something to keep in mind: just because no one’s speaking up, doesn’t mean everyone agrees. Silence isn’t always a sign that things are fine. Real communication means being active—asking questions, making sure you understand, and leaving room for people to disagree. It’s about realizing that everyone sees things a little differently, and that those differences can actually make your team stronger, not weaker.
When teams make a real effort to build trust and open up communication from the start, they’re so much better equipped to handle setbacks, adapt to whatever comes their way, and lift each other higher. The invisible connections between them grow stronger, and that’s what turns a group of individuals into a real team.
